title: In Defense of Jenny Jones
author: https://hedgehogreview.com/contributors/john-rosenthal
text:
If there is no freedom to act foolishly as well as wisely, there is no freedom at all.
—attributed to Senator Sam Ervin (D-NC)

In March 1995, in Lake Orion, Michigan, Jonathan Schmitz purchased a 12-gauge shotgun, drove to Scott Amedure’s trailer, and killed him. Three days earlier, both men had appeared on Jenny Jones, in a segment titled “Revealing Same-Sex Secret Crush.” Encouraged by Jenny, Amedure, who was gay, confessed to a crush on Schmitz and joked about whipped cream in a hammock. Schmitz laughed and insisted he was straight. It looked like typical tabloid foolishness, until Schmitz killed Amedure.

At trial, which the press dubbed “the Jenny Jones Murder,” Schmitz was convicted of second-degree murder and sentenced to decades in prison. Amedure’s parents were awarded $29.3 million in a wrongful-death suit against the show, although the Michigan Court of Appeals ruled the producers had no duty to foresee that Schmitz, who suffered from Graves’ disease and manic depression, would pose a threat to Amedure. Jenny herself was never named as a defendant. Ratings dipped, but the show ran for eight more years. 

For a few months in the mid-1990s, after dropping my daughter at school, I’d linger over a cup of coffee and watch Jenny Jones. Those were the glory years of tabloid TV, and just to name a few of the hosts—Ricki Lake, Maury Povich, Jerry Springer—is to recall a gilded age of TV inanity. Each host filtered American dysfunction through his or her persona—Maury possessed the charm of an avid polygraph examiner (“You’re NOT the father!”), Geraldo Rivera, a newshound in restraints, Sally Jessy Raphael, stern and schoolmarmish. 

Jenny Jones, however, was different.

I admit it: Watching Jenny Jones was a guilty pleasure. I was a photographer, a writer. Negatives were waiting in the darkroom; an essay on Diane Arbus lay unfinished. In Chapel Hill, a university town, no one I knew watched tabloid TV. My friends—teachers, poets, dancers, artists—looked wounded when I mentioned Jenny’s name. I wanted to say, “But Jenny’s not like the others,” but that would sound worse. My background didn’t help, shaped as it was during the 1960s by acting in summer-stock theaters, where high-mindedness was the least of my concerns. I had lines to learn day after day, and Charley’s Aunt and A Man for All Seasons simply blurred into each other.

Everyone, of course, watched Donahue. His experts talked about meaningful things like parenting, alcoholism, abortion, and racism. They were very sincere, and one felt sincere watching them. But they rarely said anything that surprised me. When Gloria Steinem told Donahue that the Equal Rights Amendment should be a part of the US Constitution, I agreed with her. Jenny’s guests, on the other hand, lacked any sort of expertise—I mean any—and seemed devoted only to their own rather bizarre personal problems. There was nothing particularly distinctive about them, yet I found them more interesting than Gloria Steinem. 

Unless you thought about it, Jenny Jones was just another tabloid circus. Her guests were often dramatically depressed, the audiences rowdy. Yet Jenny stood in sharp contrast to Geraldo and Sally Jessy Raphael, who, on camera, were earnest, devoid of humor, and pseudo serious. They demanded to know why their guests—say, skinheads or teenage Satanists—were so remarkably unhinged. They ferreted out the psychological, as well as scandalous facts. Were you bullied? Were your parents strict? Too strict? Geraldo, dapper like a harried headwaiter, was tenacious; Sally, steely-eyed behind red glasses, was pugnacious. They weren’t outlandish like Jerry Springer, but still, they sold titillation disguised as journalism, a very shady business, and neither of them ever suggested that just being normal isn’t all that easy.

Jenny, on the other hand, was light on interrogation. With her anodyne, quintessentially Midwestern name, her attractive yet unassuming blond look, and her high, sweet voice, she treated her guests—bullies, teenage strippers, cheating spouses, monumentally overweight and embarrassing mothers—as entertainment, not social pathology. This isn’t honorable, but neither is a carnival. Her gift was to be both above the fray and in it—an angel granting the fifteen minutes of fame her seemingly unhappy guests craved.

Sometimes, while I watched the show, I took notes, which I recently found in an old notebook. It was supposed to be an essay laced with irony, but since I never wrote it, I must have lacked faith in my own condescension. Now, three decades later, living in a society overwhelmed by online pornography, menaced by militant neo-Nazis, and numbed by unthinkably coarse political rhetoric, I remember Jenny Jones as a rather innocent way to waste a little time. 

Jenny’s shows often had titles that left little to the imagination, e.g., “You Say That Body’s Home Grown, But I Know It’s All Silicone.” Or the metrically damaged yet effectively off-balance, “Zits, Pimples, and Algebra Books, I Was a Nerd Then but Now Guys Love My Looks!”

One episode must have caught my attention, because I described the entire segment. (This was before DVR technology.) It was starkly titled “Clean Up Your Act or Get Out!” and featured two couples facing the same dilemma: one partner messy, the other neat. Jenny introduced us to one tidy partner first, a pale, exhausted-looking woman named Cindi, who told domestic horror stories about toothpaste tubes left open and crumbs in the bed. Jenny, dressed in a cute salmon-pink suit and wearing sparkling earrings, knew how to elicit sympathy for this vexed young woman. Jenny asked if Ken, Cindi’s boyfriend, “ever ever” picked up his clothes, or vacuumed? No, never. Jenny’s voice sounded a note of winking outrage. Does he ever make the bed? No. Never. According to Cindi, “Ken believes making beds and vacuuming is ‘women’s work.’” The audience erupted in boos. 

I’m sure I laughed. Poor Ken. No doubt, I was remembering the early 1970s, when the women’s liberation movement unsettled everything. In Chapel Hill, most of the educated women I knew had joined “consciousness-raising” groups whose core texts included The Feminine Mystique and The Second Sex. These groups transformed suspicion into fact: Women were exploited professionally and personally. Men like me were caught off-guard. I wasn’t a pig. I cleaned up after myself. I changed diapers. But raised by a loving mother who wanted me to be happy, I often acted as if I had the world on a string. Unacceptable. Women castigated me for loving Henry Miller. One defaced my copy of Norman Mailer’s Advertisements for Myself, scratching on its title page “THIS BOOK DEGRADES WOMEN!” Humor between the sexes vanished. Men who left dishes in the sink were “unevolved.” Marriages ended—mine and many others. Now a studio audience who’d never heard of Kate Millett was booing the very idea of domestic inequality.

Tragedy had turned into farce. 

Cindi then confided that Ken hadn’t brushed his teeth or changed his underwear in a month, which is why she would not kiss him anymore and had postponed their wedding. The audience, already on her side, applauded wildly. They also cheered when introduced to the second tidy partner, Lance, a bulldog of a guy with very sad eyes, who said that he wouldn’t marry his fiancée, Heather, until she rinsed the tub after her weekly bath. He described the ring of grime, and the audience groaned in unison.

Naturally, after hearing grievances from these oppressed partners, we were eager to meet their oppressors. Following her interviews with Cindi and Lance, Jenny shouted, “Now, let’s meet Ken!” A glittering wall panel lifted, and there was Ken, in electric-blue darkness, laughing defiantly and punching the air like Rocky. The audience roared its approval. Ken was everything I’d hoped—overweight, unshaven, with long, oily hair, looking like he’d slept in a field. And, sad to say, so did Heather, introduced seconds later, a large woman with pouchy eyes and wild hair, who ran down the ramp pumping her arms up and down to fervent applause.

This was close to insanity. Within seconds, outrage over Ken’s slovenliness had turned into approval. I think I understand why. Ken may have been the swinish fiancé from hell, but he believed in himself—and what could matter more? For years, TV psychologists like Dr. Joyce Brothers had championed self-esteem as the ultimate virtue—the key to happiness and success. Positive reinforcement had become an American passion—a patriotism of the self. Clumsy children who played games badly, who made their teammates groan, were given trophies just for…being on the team! Playing badly was OK. Not just OK, it was great! (Though nobody was fooled.) Naturally Jenny’s audience forgot that Ken, basking in neon-lit self-affirmation, was, at bottom, just a top-tier slob.

Well, this was television—entertainment, not an interrogation—and even if Lance and Cindi looked seriously woebegone, there was no reason to believe them. They were on television, and we weren’t. 

Anyway, who cared? Television is a mesmeric medium that dissolves judgment in a crucible of visual immediacy. It creates a free-floating tolerance for everything. This is the message of the medium. Even though, as a boy, I’d learned in school (which is a medium) that killing someone was a crime, and in church (the same) that it was a sin, I never questioned the right of happily married cowboys, like Roy Rogers, to shoot someone if necessary. At age fifteen, my favorite show was Mike Hammer, and I think Darren McGavin killed somebody once a week. 

Ken’s honeymoon with the audience didn’t last. Once he joined Cindi and the other couples onstage, Jenny showed videotapes of Ken and Cindi’s home. These tapes documented a pathology of filth: half-eaten TV dinners beside overflowing ashtrays, beer cans strewn over an orange shag carpet, crusty dishes piled high in the sink. 

Sitting in my bright kitchen, with its clean counters, I asked myself, “Are these people insane?”

The audience began to groan again. 

And Lance and Heather’s apartment looked much the same. 

In her high, plaintive voice, Jenny asked, “Heather, with so many beer cans on the floor, how do you get from one room to the other?”

Heather’s reply was suspiciously perfect. 

“You’ve got to stay on the path.”

Watching TV is simple, but thinking about it isn’t. Cindi and Ken seemed to have lived hapless lives without the advantages I took for granted. They were, to all appearances, losers, the first sign of which was a near-total disregard for basic rules of grooming. From my perch of respectability (and income), I wondered if I should laugh or feel sorry for them? After all, I’m a photographer. How the other half lives has always been a central concern of photography. Ask any documentary photographer how often his subjects could afford a Leica.

When I was a boy, I’d watch my mother sort through clothes I’d outgrown—my corduroy pants and flannel shirts—and take them to her church, where they would be distributed to “underprivileged children.” I wondered who these children were. Did they line up to be handed my clothes? I felt a little sorry for them, or tried to. In New Rochelle, in my fifth-grade class at Stephenson School, I knew city kids who talked dirty, couldn’t sit still, and had their own scent. Their clothes looked worn. Unruly children, nonreaders, often daredevils, and, from my point of view, fascinating. They didn’t live in a large white house like I did, but I didn’t think of them as underprivileged. On the contrary, they seemed to possess privileged information about the world—unpleasant information that I tried to ignore. When watching Jenny Jones, I wondered if Ken, Cindi, Lance, and Heather had been underprivileged children who had grown up but still delivered bad news.

Unlike Geraldo Rivera and Sally Jessy Raphael, TV veterans who treated their guests with a creepy journalistic curiosity, Jenny, like a hostess at a party for social misfits, found amusement in her guests’ problems and eccentricities. She didn’t seem to be above them. Critics mistook this familiarity as a flaw, as if Jenny’s show wasn’t serious enough. But in defense of the lighter touch, I should note that Jenny never condescended to her guests, or treated them as damaged goods, or, even worse, intriguing specimens. Geraldo, with his law degree from Brooklyn Law School, most assuredly didn’t want to be seen as a barker selling glimpses of “Men in Lace Panties”—but that’s exactly what he was.

If Jenny’s rapport with her guests was easy and familiar, if she rarely wore a concerned look, the reason wasn’t mysterious: Jenny was a creation of show business. She had no experience in broadcasting or journalism. No college degree. Not even a high school degree. She wasn’t even Jenny Jones.

Born Janina Stronski, she spent an unloving childhood in London, Ontario, shoplifting, running away from home, drinking heavily, and touring mining towns in her own rock band. At age eighteen, she ditched her unmarketable Polish name for “Jenny Jones,” moved to LA, worked as a hostess at a strip club, and later landed in Las Vegas as a drummer in an all-girl rock band, singing backup for Wayne Newton. Reinventing herself yet again, she turned to standup comedy and became a platinum blond in a miniskirt, delivering clever punch lines about older husbands (“We played Hide the Insulin”) and cheap dates (“At least he was a gentleman—he took me to a restaurant and carried my tray”).

Jenny was funny.

And yet, though Jenny was a product of show business, you wouldn’t know it. After thirty unglamorous years spent on the lower rungs of the industry, she looked like an attractive suburban housewife who’d just slipped one of her famous apple pies into the oven. Her comic timing was impeccable, and, apparently, the market was ready for a talk show with a softer edge. I can easily picture the Time Warner executive at a conference table, hands out like he was holding a melon. “Funny. Pretty. Relatable! What’s not to like about this package?”

The original format of Jenny Jones was tailored to women—hair, makeup, cooking, and bad boyfriends. However, by the time I tuned in, the show had gone tabloid and included not only retro musical acts and makeovers but also ridiculously dysfunctional couples looking for their fifteen minutes of fame. Who better to offer it to them than Jenny, who once said, “Show business was my way out.”

After her guests were (sort of) interviewed, Jenny would stroll into the audience, microphone in hand, and invite questions (my favorite part of the show). Given the excitability of tabloid studio audiences, it was always a gamble. Yet the questions directed at Ken and Heather struck a balance between insulting and reasonable: “How can you live in such squalor and maintain your self-respect?” And: “How can you claim to love someone and then treat them so inconsiderately?” These questions, holier-than-thou in nature, bounced off Ken and Heather, who were champions of self-empowerment. Rule number one: Never let the expectations of others define you. “Hey,” Ken crowed, echoing Sammy Davis Jr., “I gotta be me!” And Heather, turning to Lance, declared, “If your friends don’t like coming over, if the place is too messy for them, they can take a hike!” Needless to say, the audience applauded both the questions and the answers.

Sometimes things didn’t go smoothly. On one episode, titled “I Got No Shame, ’Cuz My Chest Gives Me All Game,” Jasmine, a young woman with gingery hair, wearing a little red sling that barely covered her, said she wore sexy tops to get free drinks from bartenders. This remark, in its forthright decadence, riled the audience, and a woman, plain as a stick, took the mike and screeched, “If you act like trash, you are trash!” Jasmine stood up, gave the woman a withering look, and yelled back, “Honey, if you got it, flaunt it!” The audience applauded rapturously. A friend of Jasmine insisted—plausibly—that women shouldn’t define themselves as just a body; after all, everybody has a mind too. The audience agreed, but the applause was light. 

Admittedly, this is ridiculous stuff—the boos, the jeers, the buffoonery, and the belligerent self-exposure. My friends in Chapel Hill would disapprove, but would Shakespeare? A third of Shakespeare’s audience consisted of laborers and apprentices who paid a penny to stand in the muddy pit of the Globe. During performances, they drank ale and ate oranges and nuts. Sometimes, if they liked or disliked a play or a performance, they threw food at the stage. Shakespeare knew his audience. They were inseparable from the air he breathed. He gave them Falstaff.

Watching Jenny Jones, I often sensed how little stood between Jenny’s shallow guests and the characters in serious drama. Is it so difficult to imagine Uncle Vanya as one of Jenny’s guests? Farce is just drama in clown shoes. Onstage, Vanya despairs: My life is wasted! The Professor is a fraud! Yelena doesn’t love me! But as a guest on Jenny’s stage, he could easily be taken for a compulsively obnoxious man in a severe midlife crisis.

One of Jenny’s gifts was her ability to pacify her fractious kingdom. Her secret weapon was projecting photographs of her guests as toddlers. Instantly, the audience would quiet down and begin to coo. There was Ken, a wisp of a boy, grinning and toddling around in a plastic pool. And Heather—a delicate, blond, five-year-old girl—arms outspread, bouncing on a bed. I think the cooing drowned out the question foremost in our minds: What catastrophic event had transformed those angelic children into the hulking, unabashedly offensive adults who took pride in living like swine? Photographs are not static—they drift between past and present. They comfort us when they preserve continuity, but they unnerve us when they reveal the havoc of history.

Yet whatever questions the photographs evoked were beside the point, since it was time for the “Makeover.” I caught only one segment of “Radical Makeover.” It felt like something only women would enjoy—a celebration of cosmetics and appearance. I’d forgotten how, as a child, I’d watch my mother put on her face before heading to a cocktail party or the grocery store. Back then, with no concept of a presentable self, I believed the meticulously arranged objects on her vanity—golden tubes of lipstick, soft brushes, gem-like perfume bottles—held secrets as deep as Aladdin’s lamp.

The segment was called “Goth-Girl Makeover”—a paradox, since the point of being goth is to look like one. I wondered if she was an ironic goth who’d maxed out on cemeteries and wanted to sit around with her dad and listen to Billy Joel.

When this multi-pierced teen first appeared, dressed in a spooky little outfit, she looked bloodless, as if recently disinterred. The audience reaction was mixed and loud. She was booed as a child no parent would wish for but applauded as someone who’d made her Halloween dreams come true.

Half an hour later, post-makeover, she looked like a young lawyer with an upscale future. Was she pleased? Hard to say. As the audience cheered, she looked tentative, like someone beginning to feel the effects of radiation. But that was OK. These things take time.

What mattered was that her makeover offered a television truth: that despair, dysfunction, and social resentment might just be a “look” gone rogue. Even if it’s not true, I admire the idea—for surely that young woman in the tailored suit and green silk scarf lightly thrown over her shoulder made more human sense to me than the goth girl in her leather dog collar and black lipstick, her eyes dulled by an unexamined affection for Death.

In October 1995, a few months after I’d stopped watching Jenny’s show, Democratic Senator Joe Lieberman and Republican William Bennett held a bipartisan press conference condemning the frivolity and rampant sexuality of daytime tabloid talk shows where “indecent exposure is celebrated as a virtue.” Calling their stance “a revolt of the revolted,” they cited—as if they were picking up a used handkerchief—a segment of Sally Jessy Raphael in which a father who had molested his daughter apologized and offered her a bouquet of roses. Invoking “decent, average Americans,” they urged sponsors such as Kraft and Procter & Gamble to reconsider advertising on shows that perpetuated “cultural rot.”

But in the 1990s, the concept of “decent, average Americans” was hard to parse. Wasn’t it the “average” American who watched tabloid TV? And if so, what did “decent” mean? Did Bennett and Lieberman really think Gen-Xers and Millennials longed for the patriarchal clarity of Ward Cleaver? If they’d been even halfway serious, they’d have known that America didn’t need saving from Maury Povich or Jenny Jones. It needed saving from Seinfeld.

Seinfeld was revolutionary. It broke sitcom norms that required characters to learn, mature, or at least think. In M*A*S*H, Hawkeye savaged military bureaucracy, but he still saved lives. Archie Bunker’s panoramic bigotry was tempered by empathy. In both shows, self-reflection surfaced, however briefly. But in Seinfeld, there was no heartfelt resolutions. Nobody learned from their mistakes. To Jerry, George, and Elaine, love was neurosis, friendship was disposable, and altruism nonexistent. Petty annoyances became epic dramas while real ethical dilemmas—love, politics, family—were punch lines. Kramer’s frenetic entrances added a slapstick touch to what was otherwise an endless kvetch.

Seinfeld was outrageously funny, but even Chuck Klosterman, who admired Seinfeld’s lethal critique of urban life, was right to call it “the most villainous sitcom ever made.”

It also had more than nineteen million viewers. 

Bennett and Lieberman styled themselves defenders of the civilized world, but they were, at heart, East Coast snobs of the Yale-Harvard variety. Tabloid TV wasn’t tailored to the sensibilities of the educated elite but to the Midwest’s large working class, who preferred the drama of confrontation (upset people yelling) to Letterman’s cool detachment or the ironic nihilism of Seinfeld. 

So I watched Jenny Jones until its formula, like any formula, wore thin. Still, I missed the “Totally Useless Talents” segments: the girl who could drink milk and expel it out of her tear ducts, or the guy who sucked an egg yolk up his nostril.

Despite the fleeting but damaging publicity from the Jonathan Schmitz trial, Jenny Jones lasted another eight years. But by the early 2000s, tabloid talk shows began to lose ground to reality TV. These new shows offered tense, mostly unscripted drama with the voyeuristic spectacle of an unraveling—now with prize money.

But something else was happening. After 9/11, as terrorists began to haunt the national imagination, America grew less inclined to openly ridicule. A new wellness movement arrived, ushering in reams of self-help books and a new TV paradigm led by Oprah and Dr. Phil: the tabloid talk show as therapeutic theater. Guests were no longer ridiculed; they were to be understood by pop psychologists like Dr. Phil. Instead of caricatures—men in diapers, obstreperous moms in hot pants—guests were framed as survivors of human misfortune: domestic violence, child abuse, addiction, cancer, OCD, even medical malpractice. Dr. Phil and Oprah didn’t look frivolous like Jenny or smarmy like Geraldo, but their lavish sincerity was engineered to sell products. 

The need to ridicule may change its shape over time, but it never disappears. Call it the tabloid spirit. To Plautus, the Roman satirist, the Other consisted of scolding women, effeminate foreigners, and supercilious old men. To Jenny’s producers, it was rebellious teens, embarrassing boyfriends, and cross-dressers. Nothing new. Both ridicule the Other as a means of upholding the status quo, which, to our consternation, is always in the process of becoming a new status quo. Even though Dr. Phil and Oprah diluted trash TV under the guise of “healing,” the shaming instinct (the scarlet letter) never vanished. It just held its breath. 

Now, more than twenty-five years later, Jenny Jones figures as one small, festive element in a rather free-spirited time in my life. This may be the soft-focus amnesia of nostalgia, but still, one should be honest about what time takes away. In 1994, my parents and my brother and all my close friends were still alive. My daughter was ten, in love with Broadway musicals. There was a puppy around, and my wife and I were middle-aged and healthy. 

In any case, I have no problem defending the frivolity that Jenny Jones represented. I believe in frivolity. I’m all for it. I favor the vulgar. Frivolity, in my mind, is the great escape from the mock seriousness of the middle class and its sensitive chatter. Though I was raised firmly in that class (my father was an attorney with offices at Rockefeller Center), my heart was treasonous. 

Yet if lightheartedness refers only to itself, which, being light, doesn’t weigh very much, what is the meaning of dark-heartedness?

To answer that question, one need only watch a couple episodes of the reality series The Apprentice, in which youngish MBA types with the moral depth of slot machines competed for a chance to join the Trump Organization. The guiding mythos of the show—hyper-capitalism itself—was staged as a morality play in which self-promotion and ruthless strategizing were rewarded as virtues. No space was allotted to humane thoughtfulness. Or to humor. It was pure jungle beneath the business casual. True to its tabloid roots, the show’s iconic moment—its only iconic moment—was a televised ritual of humiliation. Donald Trump, real-estate mogul, sits majestically in a dimly lit boardroom. Occasionally, Ivanka, his moon-faced daughter, sits beside him. Background music hums with menace. Someone on the team has shown poor leadership. A pricing strategy misfired. A pitch missed. The team, an almost illegally dislikable crew, argues among themselves. (One can’t imagine them as children in a wading pool.) Trump raises his hands, signaling enough. He points at the expendable contestant and declares, “You’re fired! Go!” Moments later, the loser is escorted out of the building to a waiting taxi. Exciting TV, yet repellent. It was dark-hearted.

A mood had slipped away.

Tabloid TV, which made a living ridiculing preposterous guests, faded out at the same time that progressive ideologues in colleges, corporations, and government agencies began to replace even faintly offensive words with ungainly euphemisms. Among ethical purists, there’s no room for ribbing. What’s funny, they ask, about a short person being called “short”? A better question is, What’s funny about all of us? And the answer is, plenty. We are all, in our special ways, ridiculous. The deeper irony is that David Foster Wallace was right—the “Orwellian substitution of the euphemisms of social equality for social equality itself” was a gift to conservatives. They delighted in watching progressives fret over how to describe someone rather than constructing legislation that would effectively redistribute America’s wealth. What did word choice have to do with factories closing in Pennsylvania and reopening in China? 

It’s easy to dismiss tabloid TV as lowbrow entertainment, and yet its jeering note found an echo in the tone of progressive ideology. Wokeness, impervious to nuance, claimed the high ground, but its very name insulted those it intended to wake. As it turned out, the unwoke, who, electorally, were non-college voters, didn’t welcome the news that their everyday speech was offensive and their lives were defined by “cis” privilege. They felt insulted. Looked down upon. That is a fundamental mistake righteous reformers make, a paradox born of moral urgency, for which a terrible price is usually paid.

The price of course was the two presidencies of Donald Trump—a backlash that flattened any and all progressive “corrections” of the past thirty years. Nor was it irrelevant that Trump was heir to the tabloid tradition that thrived on mockery and humiliation. (“You’re fired!” was just an early version of “Drain the swamp!”) In the 2015 Republican debates, Trump brought derision and name‑calling onto the political stage, sweeping aside the nine other candidates, who spoke in canned platitudes. His political genius was to adopt the stance of a gladiator for those who felt overlooked in the new global order and were tired of minding their pronouns.

Certainly, it’s beyond the scope of this essay to address Trump’s desire to restore an old racial hierarchy and undermine the elite infrastructure of American life—its science, arts, and bureaucratic expertise. My subject is tabloid TV, or, rather, the spirit of it, which, I believe, Trump embodies to a remarkable degree. He is at once the defiant, narcissistic guest and the outraged, heckling audience. Successful demagogues know instinctively that in order to “read” the room, you must become the room. 

And what a surprising world we live in! Those days when my friends looked down upon the clownishly bad manners of tabloid TV seem to have occurred on another planet. In Trump’s USA, they strain to find the ugliest names—and some are truly ugly—to describe the man they detest. So much for middle-class refinement.

And it is about mood, isn’t it? Those Jenny Jones days of raucous public mirth seem, in retrospect, almost tame and good-natured. Entertainment steeped in derision has always survived reformers eager to make us gentler than we are. But the hard truth remains: We are pretty good, but not great. Never great. Despite Jonathan Schmitz’s derangement and William Bennett’s finger‑wagging, those days—when guests and audience members traded mockery, when laughter felt communal, when toddler photos recalled a lost innocence—are not to be dismissed. For let’s face it, Ken and Cindi were always going to get married. There was never any doubt. The studio audience knew it. I knew it. Jenny knew it. We simply played at not knowing it. Ken was a slob, Cindi wasn’t, but they knew that if they brought their mess onto Jenny Jones, it would become, wonderfully, their mess—and they’d have something to laugh about for years. It was silly, ridiculous, and funny without consequence. These were not important people. None of us were.
